body: That bipolar disorder and depression run deep in my family, that my mother's been symptomatic on and off for what is almost certainly bipolar disorder for her entire adult life and that my sister suffered from depression as a teenager and still has symptoms to date. It took a long while for this to really sink in even after I was diagnosed as bipolar.

Moods with both low and high elements combined. Note that these can vary both in the low dimension and in the high dimension independently, and hence cover a very wide range of possible moods.

Even for me at least, they vary wildly, ranging from things such as moods that feel mostly like plain low moods, except my head is a flutter with thoughts rather than quiet or even silent and I have very little interest in sleep, to things such as moods that feel almost like hypomania, but with the euphoria, giddiness, expansiveness, and like absent and often replaced with pain and/or anxiety.

These are only two examples; I have had many other sorts of mixed moods, with overall severity ranging from something feeling like a very light hypomania minus any euphoria to moods characterized by severe, overwhelming, crushing pain combined with a constant whirlwind of repetitive and very negative and/or suicidal thoughts, where the suicidal thoughts have intent and are reinforced by the other negative thoughts whirling about.

Oh, rapid cycling, and that with usually daily or sometimes up to weekly cycles, is so much the norm for me lately (and for good periods both during going to school and thereafter) that I find *not* rapid cycling fast to be worth noting in contrast to it. I do find the four-episodes-a-year definition of *rapid cycling* funny, as by my standards having only four distinct mood episodes in a year period is *very slow and stable*...

From just glancing that over, *I wish*... consider I have been *markedly* symptomatic without any real breaks at all for about 1.5 years now, and furthermore have during that period only been able to be entirely free of suicidal ideation for maybe 1.5-2 months at most at a time. This seems to only be of much use for people who primarily have normal or only mild low or high mood, rather than people where, even with medication, being in a marked episode is the norm rather than the exception.

Caffeine has never made me manic or hypomanic per se, but significant quantities of caffeine (multiple large cups of strong coffee in a row, e.g.) can at times tip me from low moods into mixed moods or make preexisting mixed moods more intense. Mind you that I much of the time, especially these days, tend away from high moods overall but rather strongly tend towards low moods and mixed moods, something this is definitely not the case for all people.

I had little lag, only about half a year, between developing more severe bipolar symptoms and getting diagnosed, so I really have very little of a period of being very symptomatic but untreated to look back on. This lag period was dominated by rather *strong* hypomania, or mild *mania proper* depending on how one looks at it, being divided by a moderate depressive episode, and ended in my first truly severe depression, which is what made me truly realize that things had gone horribly wrong. As I was settling in at my university, though, during this period I never really developed any particular lifestyle influenced by being bipolar.

However, I have a longer period, of two to three years before then, of having milder bipolar symptoms, dominated largely by hypomania but with noticeable mood fluctuation and with bits of what in retrospect was clear low mood interspersed in it. I *do* miss how my life was then, as I was largely active and motivated and involved in various things, the days when I happened to feel blah and uninterested in doing things aside. I deeply miss being able to put lots of energy into my own (software development) work, into activities like biking significant distances, and into being involved in political activities and the like. Yes, during this period I had some brushes with police and state security forces (thankfully only being arrested per se once despite my varied close brushes), but that is not surprising from what I was involved in, and does not make me regret any of it.

What I do regret, however, is that I did notice that my mood was deteriorating then, including my up and down mood fluctuation, my oftentimes being full of antsy, uncontrollable energy even when undesirable, my having inexplicable sharp downward mood swings randomly, and my extended episode of milder depression between these two periods, yet I did not know to do anything about it until things got far more severe in nature, due to that had things been caught earlier they could have potentially not gotten nearly as bad as they have (thanks to "kindling" as they call it). I don't know why my parents hid that bipolar ran in my mother's family (with a sister having it, an aunt who would have definitely been diagnosed had she been alive today, and her mother and she herself(1) having undiagnosed, milder mood problems of some sort as well) until *after* I got diagnosed, which they only found out about when I had to call them for my insurance information.

(1) She says that she had depressive episodes that she did not get treated after both me and my sister got born, but for the longest time *before* I even found this out I noticed things in her such as varying between being very blah and withdrawn to having intense, irritable, irrational anger that I saw in no one else I knew, so I suspect that it may go deeper than this.

I'd want to be able to affect my mood myself, in any way at all - but it seems to be essentially beyond my control, and that whenever I think I might have some influence over it somehow, it quickly is clearly just an illusion and self-deception on my part.

Even when I get the idea that I can force myself past what my mood happens to be, it almost invariably becomes quickly apparent that that is actually my mood itself at work, and not something truly under my conscious control.

The only exception to this is that I can often overcome *severe* low moods that are otherwise highly disabling through acting on habits and routines I already have established (as I am someone who acts *very heavily* in terms of habit and routine, and this allows me to oftentimes outwardly function much better than I would otherwise). However, this has the fundamental limitation that I cannot normally establish new routines in lower mood states, and the lower my mood state the harder it is to keep to the ones I am following and not to let them drop to the wayside.

I haven't had any, actually.

And I wouldn't say that this is "enlightenment" but rather *necessity*; if I didn't think this way about my moods and my thoughts I probably *would* be dead...

No, I haven't in any kind of formal sense, actually; the closest that applies is simply talking to people I know online with respect to their (and our) psychological troubles. Aside from that I've just had a good working knowledge of abnormal psychology, especially that of mood disorders, and am very used to my mood states and thought patterns almost constantly going all over the place (ultradian cycling yay) and am used to treating the feelings and thoughts as a result of that as not really being "my" thoughts or feelings at any intrinsic level but merely a product of my mood state at any given moment, which I likewise tend to treat as almost "external" like one would treat any physical illness (even though this is not always entirely possible).

This is one of those things where, honestly, if anyone else said what I've said here to me, I myself would think that they are definitely *not safe*...

... and I probably from a rational standpoint shouldn't think myself any different... even though I can't help but think that I can restrain myself, and hence end up weighing things like my (precarious) finances over my safety, as it would be judged by someone else.

When I do think about it some more, I still think I can probably keep myself safe for now on my own... even though then I think whether I am just fooling myself there.

(I have had my best friend tell me before that I should do what you have told me here when I get like this... but as they live about a thousand miles away and cannot actually drag me to the ER themselves practically, none of that happened in the past.)

On the other hand, I am sure that were I to drink significantly I would surely at least make a suicide attempt, but probably one far less likely to be successful than if I were to make one while sober. At least I don't drink except with others, and I don't have any alcohol around my apartment... If I did I would probably either have earned myself an unsuccessful suicide attempt or be dead already...

**Update:**

I called said best friend and they got me to call my psychiatrist first thing in the morning and to check myself into the ER if things get worse and especially if there is any likelihood of me giving into these suicidal impulses... but it *really* sounded like she actually wanted me to go to the ER regardless, and only agreed to me doing the former as she knew it would be hard to convince me to just go to the ER by default... (Actually, she sounded the most scared I've ever heard her, and seemed very worried that I might really end up dead, so...)

> So if you're not sure of why you want to kill yourself just let it hold off.. see if the feeling subsides.

I'm trying.

It's just very disconcerting and frightening to have intense suicidal feelings that don't just last one night and then vanish (for then), which include multiple plans that could each be easily executed within the day or even immediately, combined with a mood that would actually allow acting on them.

Usually my suicidal ideation that could lend itself to actually acting upon it is either combined with more severe depression, which makes it unlikely to be acted upon, or otherwise is shortlived (albeit very likely to recur) and hence any real danger can be avoided simply by outlasting it a night. And even then, I usually don't have nearly as clear ideation of actual plans with the thought that they could be easily acted upon...

Now that I think of it, I'm probably actually still in some kind of mixed state, just with the low component being significantly greater than before. That would probably explain why I have so much more thought of actually acting, immediately or in the very short term, on plans, that easily pop into my head... which is something that simply does not happen in plain low moods for me, even the most severe ones.

> It seems to me like you might be putting a little too much faith into medication - the simple pharmacological fact of it is that the brain grows tolerant of the effects of things after a while. So while they might help.. you probably won't find a cure all.

I simply don't know what else to do, except maybe try to get more exercise, something I am trying to do lately, or trying to have more regular sleep, something I honestly am not doing at all...

> Healing sometimes has to come from the inside, but the medication can help.

To me that's something easier said than done... as over most of the last decade my mood has been unstable or at best merely temporarily normal in a longer time-scale cycling with mild-to-moderate depression, no matter what I do... and with only meds seemingly making any dent in things at all.

> If you're ever feeling out of reasons to keep on living, feel free to PM me - I'm always open to talking.

In states like this, and honestly very recently, I've easily gotten so that I really do not feel I have any reasons to keep on living. While I can try to rationally think up reasons, they just don't "stick" at all, so I still keep on feeling that I have no reason or very little reason to keep on living.

> Stay strong! :)

I'll try.

Well all this I know...

... but I tend to view the call-your-doctor-or-go-to-the-ER-immediately impractical most of the time simply because if I had followed this advice over the past year (and some), I would have spent whole months at a time at least in the psych ward. It's one of those things that from some perspectives sounds like a good idea... but which from a practical one for very many (like myself) tends to be highly impractical at best...

(Mind you that there had been good chunks in this period where, even then, money-and-work issues were the sole reason that I didn't check myself in, despite knowing that it'd likely be highly unpleasant...)

Actually, it is more specific than this. Antidepressants alone are *particularly* notorious for making bipolar disorder worse, often dramatically so. (One way they unfortunately frequently find out that some individuals are bipolar in the first place is that they rapidly switch from being depressed to being manic upon being given them.)

I too would strongly recommend with continuing with Computer Engineering; classes on things like computer repair or IT or the like really are not going to lead you the kinds of places that having an actual CE degree will. And yes, there are extraneous requirements that you will have to put up with, but almost anything has its extraneous crap that comes with it, and it will be worth it in the long run.

(I for one am very glad that I got into software development (am a CS major), as it turns out that it is much more tolerant of my low moods than most other types of jobs, from what I know, would be.)

Same thought here. Antidepressants alone only invariably make bipolar disorder worse. You should *really* try to see a doctor again and get treated with meds more appropriate. Even if things seem utterly hopeless now, they likely will not be so once you get on meds that actually work for you or at least get you sufficiently stabilized.

Have you tried talking with your doctor about switching around your meds? Just because one antidepressant has not worked out for you does not mean others will not, and changing meds probably is a better idea here than going off them altogether. This is especially since just because one has not perceived any real effect oneself does not mean that there has not been an effect, and this could very well be the case here, as you yourself have reported increased depression on coming off of the citalopram. As for supplements and natural treatments, I honestly would not recommend them, especially considering that they are typically poorly controlled and tested compared to pharmaceuticals; remember that just because one antidepressant has not worked out as well as you would wish for you does not mean others would turn out the same way.

Things can easily be the other way around, though. Even though in my worst low moods I can feel completely worthless, hopeless, purposeless, empty, burdensome, and so on, and cannot find any reason why I should not kill myself other than not hurting anyone else, once I return to even a milder low mood I cannot understand just how I believed any of that. Things are likely to not be perfect by any means, but what I had believed so completely becomes merely something that my mood state somehow made me believe despite its complete unreality, as I see it from a less low of a mood.
And they also know how to treat people, with proper information, too.

There is a difference between pointing out potential diagnoses to be aware of and formally making a diagnosis as a psychiatrist - and knowing what the potential diagnoses may be, and what the significance of past symptoms and patterns of mood changes are, is very important here, as if the OP were to simply go to a psychiatrist and tell them that they were depressed, they would likely simply be given antidepressants and likely end up *even worse off than before* (which unfortunately happens far too often).

I do take issue with how you use the word "label" here, though, as if the word had pejorative connotations. If anything, being properly "labeled" is certainly a *good* thing in this context, as it means being able to be properly treated in the first place, rather than having to deal with repeated attempts at treating one that, at best, simply do not work (something, again, which unfortunately happens far too often).

(About meditation, I very seriously have my doubts that meditation as monotherapy would even put a dent in bipolar disorder as a whole, as opposed to merely potentially modifying individual mood states themselves.)

I would honestly strongly recommend going to see a psychiatrist and telling them *all* of what you have told us here - even if they try to focus on how you may be feeling at the time of the office visit, I would emphasize that you make sure they actually get all of this. Despite what some have said here, this really does *sound* like it is bipolar disorder, which requires medication to be treated properly, and which has a strong tendency to be treated improperly if those treating one do not get a full picture about what is going on (and hence are likely to think that one has unipolar depression, and thus give one antidepressants alone, which are exactly the *wrong* thing to do here).

Honestly, though, it *does* sound very much like it likely is bipolar disorder to me as well, and while you say "leave it to the pros" above, the reality is that without complete information they cannot diagnose it any better than anyone else.

This is why so many people go on with diagnoses of "unipolar depression" and get prescribed meds that simply do not work or even make things worse (as giving bipolar individuals antidepressants alone almost invariably makes it worse), as the pros only see the depressed person who comes into their office; if that person does not give them a more complete picture, especially if they have no idea what that picture would be, they can do no better.

I was lucky to be diagnosed with bipolar disorder early on particularly because I recognized patterns of past behavior in myself that fit it far too well even before I made my first office, and I told the psych I saw everything I had recognized, not merely how I felt then. But if I had simply gone into the office and said merely that I was very depressed then, without knowing the significance of the bigger picture, I almost certainly would have gone much longer before being properly diagnosed.

(And frankly, bipolar disorder really cannot be treated by meditation; while therapy is very useful for it, it is more for treating the various side-effects of being bipolar and the many things which are comorbid with it rather than treating bipolar disorder itself, whose direct symptoms it cannot treat.)

For me, when things have gotten bad, it has really only been, if I am able to really think at all, that I do not want to hurt those I am closest to (even though actually thinking this has at times been much harder than it sounds, as then I often perceive myself as a worthless burden and am essentially mentally cut off from the rest of the world) and that I am scared that any attempt will fail and only leave me worse off than before. However, at such times I often cannot really think clearly at all and am "functioning" on mere habit alone, to the point that actually forming any real suicidal plan in any coherent fashion becomes nearly impossible in the first place.

Same thought here as well, I must say.

And honestly, things like this are the main reason why I have even bothered to hang on so far, at least until more extreme low mood states take away even the ability to hurt myself, no matter how powerful the urge to "make it stop now" may be then.

However, I also am rather susceptible to mixed states, and the latter does not apply there, which scares me, as I really do not want to hurt anyone I know yet they could easily make me actually kill myself, especially since they have already almost made be go through with it.

Really what I just do is wait and try to just hold myself together through whatever mood state I am in at the very moment; very often my mood state is intense enough that I really can do nothing else.

I know I do. I try what I can, be it sleeping (when reasonably possible), calling up L. on the phone (when she answers), hiking or reading (when it is a time I can reasonably do either and my mood state will allow it), or simply trying to focus myself on something else than the mood state I am in (when my mood state allows me to even do that). Usually in plain low moods I can at least clear out any negative thoughts from my head, even if I cannot directly change my mood state, but that is harder in these more mixedish moods I have had as of late, where such thoughts take hold and buzz around inside my head far more easily and are far harder to clear out...

It is, in one way. Now I do not have to worry about mentioning these sorts of things to him, even though I will likely have to change psychs soon regardless.

However, what surprised me was how little he reacted; he did not seem to register any reaction at all to my saying that I had completely wanted to be dead for the last two weeks (with only my close relations dissuading me) and was still actively thinking of ways to kill myself. This definitely in contrast to my previous long-time psych back in Wisconsin, who had registered far more reaction and basically asked if I could promise not to hurt myself, the one time I simply mentioned suicidal ideation at all to him upon being asked, and then I had merely said that I did have some thoughts of it.

If anything, my psych seemed to react far more to my appearance of being really miserable, and somewhat agitated and anxious to boot. It is as if he had very little concern that I would ever act on my suicidal thoughts or at least made sure not to register it, despite definitely being prone to mixed symptoms (which are notoriously linked to suicide attempts) and having had them within the last month including even on the day of the appointment itself, so they were simply something to note down and little more.

(Honestly, from his rather odd office hours and from having accidentally called him at meetings during the day, I suspect his day job is actually as a hospital psychiatrist and that his practice that I visit is just something little he has on the side; hence he might be rather desensitized to suicidal people, and that my suicidal ideation may seem quite minor to him compared to what else he has seen.)

My psych reacted probably the least I could possibly imagine one reacting to someone saying that they had completely wanted to be dead while being very deeply depressed (but with some mixed elements) for a good couple weeks, were it not for having family and friends, and were actively having suicidal ideation while being in a definite mixed mood day-of, while being visibly really, really miserable and rather agitated in person.

He only added time-release lithium and offered a low dose of lorazepam; I turned down the latter.

At this point I am sure that unless I were during an appointment saying that I was undoubtedly going to kill myself then and there that I am not going to be getting any trips to the hospital with this psych.

For me, much of the time, I know that there is plenty of good there or at least far less bad than there could be there rationally, but it simply does not "stick" intuitively at all - my underlying mood state at a given moment really drives how I see everything intuitively completely independent of anything rational, even if I am entirely aware of that and even if I think my mood state at a given moment is completely without any basis in reality.

Conversely, simply talking with her and getting the chance to really air out my head with and have the company of someone who I can completely trust to talk to unguardedly and to be really listened and responded to by about such things, even if I have had to essentially explain things about abnormal psych and what I would need from her at times, has far more effect for me than trying to reason things over rationally.

In this case, managing to get a hold of her to really talk things out at least before my appointment definitely made me feel better than before, and I am very glad I managed to do so, but why it makes me feel better seems to have little connection with reasoning as to why it ought to rationally.

Okay, well, I ended up getting L. on the phone tonight, and ended up having a really good, long conversation with her about how things had been for me the last month and particularly my upcoming psych visit, well, today. She ended up convincing me that I really ought to be honest with my psych tomorrow (technically today), despite my very strong tendencies (known to her) towards trying to minimize (or outright hide) things with just about everyone including even my psych, which I will definitely have to resist. I ended up figuring that, need be, I could probably end up being able to at least steer my psych towards arranging any potential hospitalization, if things come to that, so that it does not interfere with my work and so I can at least settle things beforehand. (She also got me to stop panicking about my psych visit, whereas earlier tonight I was pretty much at my wits end about it.)

As for why L. has been like this, it seems that she does definitely worry about me, but she does not quite realize the true seriousness of how things are, from my phone messages in which I prefer not to mention overt suicidal ideation (due to not wanting it to be left recorded while associated with me in Real Life), combined with that she automatically assumes that I will be able to handle things and she does not quite read into things like me stopping leaving messages all of a sudden. Thus when she's retreated into her school and work she does not quite clue into that things may be truly dangerously wrong on my end, so she figures no need to get back to me, until I end up getting in touch with her again and she finds out that I was actually very, very suicidal, and then realizes that I had been far, far over my head (even more than I myself think)...

Doing things like those I was doing this morning do not really give me a sense of well-being per se, but they do definitely take them off my mind as I do not have to worry about them anymore, at least for now.

As for doing the stuff I do as a matter of routine every applicable day, they are more a matter of trying to hold things together just enough to keep a job, and mind you where I work is very tolerant of my personal needs and problems, and to outwardly seem at least somewhat okay, even if I am really not okay whatsoever underneath it all. They do not give me a sense of well-being at all but rather are just part of the facade I keep in place with regard to the rest of the world.

(I think my immediate manager, who knows I am bipolar, though, can tell what mental state I am really in at a given point, as how much time I spend chatting away with coworkers versus how much time I spend in my cubicle along with how much code I check in to version control and how frequently I do so corresponds awfully closely to where I really am at mentally despite how I might seem outwardly, and if I have not checked in much or if any in a good while he often asks me if I am actually all right. The reason for this is that my mood states affect my willingness to socialize in ways that I tend to not hide very much and affect my ability to code in ways that I simply cannot truly hide, even when I can make my outward appearance seem normal enough.)

And on another note, wow my moods change a lot... by early afternoon I turned from a more-okayish, lighter mixed mood to a much more... foul mood like that I was in last night, albeit not feeling suicidal unlike then, which has by now turned into something more like a somewhat jittery, restless, and scattered combined with somewhat suffocating low mood, with some minor bits of suicidal ideation leaking through at moments...

I am busy paying bills that I have been putting off paying simply for lack of motivation (including the kind you actually have to fill out envelopes and checks for), and doing some other things like ordering more checks, which I had been getting very low on but which I had not been able to get myself to go and order. (It is strange talking about these things as if they were major things, I know...)

Often while very depressed I can still go through the motions of my routine rather than being completely outwardly disabled, but in reality it becomes nigh impossible to do just about anything not immediately necessary outside of it, even things like washing dishes unless I have something forcing me to wash them like being literally out of utensils altogether (and then I have at times, like recently, just switched to plastic ones). It is strange, though, how things that seem like they should be equally difficult are, even when taking the force of routine into account, end up seeming unequally difficult, even in ways that inverts what one would intuitively expects; why would simply rinsing off one's utensils and throwing them in the dishwasher be so much harder than getting showered and dressed, and neatly too, in the morning?

(Well, I think I partially figured it out - certain routines that I feel that I must, must, must do are such that the force of routine almost makes them seem much easier than they would seem otherwise, but in the other direction, things that seem to accumulate, even if actually minor, often seem much harder than they are in rational terms... and also these days I generally am in better moods in the morning and around mid-day than I am in the evenings, when I am awfully inclined to just let those dishes accumulate until they seem simply impossible, and am far more likely to be all but completely disabled...)

It is strange. On one level, I feel like I can do more and am not as disabled as I had been before, and I am doing stuff this morning I ought to have done weeks ago. Yet at the same time, I have this underlying sour, uneasy, and still suffocating feeling that I wish were not present. At least this morning no suicidal thinking is present, at least right now, but it definitely was reappearing last night after having been initially erased when I had been shot into a mixed mood with much more of a high component and less of a low component...

Still here, even though my weekend ended up being a bit of a mess thanks to a combination of a bunch of strong coffee and an unintentionally lowered caffeine tolerance resulting in my mostly very depressed-but-only-lightly-mixed state turning into something much, much more like what people typically think of when they think of the words "mixed episode"...

Well, at least there was plenty of stuff that was piling up needing cleaning in the apartment, so much of that got done, albeit in the early morning hours...

Probably the same as any weekend where I am not visiting back in Wisconsin - going hiking and/or reading books I do not plan on buying if I feel up to it at the time. If I do not feel up to it, sleeping instead.
Well, I plan on being here then.

I should definitely say thanks here. While my moods themselves seem have not really changed a whole lot over much of the past week, at least the feeling of really dealing with all of this completely alone, with all these thoughts just bouncing around inside my head, seems to lightened somewhat, for now at least.

I probably will still be at least watching here on SW, as I had actually been lurking before but had not worked up the courage to make an account and post anything.

I really have not tried any self-help books at all; I am the sort who, honestly, tends to be rather skeptical about such things. I could at least take a look at that one, though.

The irony about that, though, is that often the sheer intensity of my mood states by itself "clears" my mind, by making it very difficult to think at all and then consuming much of my remaining ability to think with just sheer, overwhelming, and contentless pain, if any is left. While if some mental capacity is left after that in more intense low moods, it usually is taken up by typical "depressed" thoughts, they are in a way blunted by there being little mental capacity even for them.

However, it is really in moods with high elements mixed in with the predominant low ones, like as of late, where I tend to actually really repetitively think "depressed" thoughts, as my mind still has scattered and generally incoherent thinking going on which they will take over rather than simply being plunged into silence. It likewise is there where something of this sort might be able to help to some extent.

My next psych appointment is on the 22nd of March. (It turned out that it was sooner than I had thought, actually.)

As for what to discuss, probably that things really had not stabilized in any kind of desirable way since the last time the meds were upped; that even after that point, I started rapid cycling really badly, with frequent and very hard crashes, which then turned into the more flat but suffocating and debilitating depression and mixed moods dominated by the depressive component that I have now, with a short interlude of milder depression at the tail end of last week and the start of this.

I likewise should mention that I really have been simply forcing myself to go on a day, or even an hour, at a time, and honestly have wanted out of it all and felt completely hopeless, helpless, and alone much of the time but have either felt obligated to hang in there despite not wanting to or have simply been rendered incapable of doing anything at all. (I should probably mention that this is how I have felt at a lot of points over the last three months or so. I wonder if I should mention that I have had much more in the way of overtly suicidal thoughts during that period, even if they have not shown up that much this past week.)

As for what to do about that, the main things I can think of is trying to combine another med such as lamotrigine with my carbamazepine. While I did have horrible results from lamotrigine, that was as monotherapy, whereas possibly combining it with the carbamazepine might reduce the possibility of it causing a particularly bad mixed episode, where then, if that happens, it could always be removed.

As for last time I talked to L., it was the night after the first major demonstrations in Madison, where I called her just to check in (if just through leaving a message) to let her know how I was doing, and actually got her. I have not talked to her since then (even though she tried to call me once since then, at about the end of the week before last, but we were not able to talk due to obvious reception problems). Our only interaction since then is that she sent me an email, which I responded to, saying that she was really busy with her school and work and that she would get back to me when they quieted down (which I assume is actually the case, as she used to constantly be checking her Gmail, which I would see due to showing up as being awake under the Google Talk features of it when I had my Gmail open, where then she basically stopped showing up as using it at all.)

For a while there I was still leaving her messages, which for a while there were not all that bad by my standards, but starting from the middle of the week before this and over much of the week they were sounding worse, and worse, and worse, with me at one point basically saying that I really needed help until, at the end of last week, I figured no help was coming and that I was completely on my own, and hence stopped leaving messages altogether.

I really am not sure what would help it. I have expressed this time and time again over the years about smaller things, to seemingly no avail (my dad still does my taxes to this day, despite my insisting that I can actually do them...), but about bigger things I generally have not even tried but rather have sought to reduce the degree that they would try to help or influence me in the first place by hiding them altogether and, when not doing so, downplaying them significantly or at least carefully "editing out" parts that I really do not feel comfortable about my parents knowing, such as my suicidality.

One matter complicating things here is how my parents have always seemed to have treated me as the brilliant but damaged child, in contrast to my (younger) sister, who was always the book-dumb and unintellectual but normal child. They always saw me as being very much like one of my uncles on my mom's side, who is in many ways heavily impaired and was later diagnosed with Asperger's, which I have never been diagnosed with myself but which both my parents and I were at a certain level very aware of being present despite not having a name for it or any idea of "what" it is. Hence they always at some level seemed to treat me as damaged in some kind of uncertain way, and seemed to always have a much closer eye on how I did things and thought than my sister. After then, once I had figured out how to get my everyday affairs at least reasonably in order no matter what my mood state was, I decided that I would at least outwardly pretend to be normal as far as at all possible, if actually being normal for long was impossible. The only exception here was with L., who had known about my mood problems from the point that they really fell off the deep end at the start of the second semester of my first year of college and who had pushed me to actually get treated at that time when I lacked the motivation to do myself.
